proposedTopics.title: Safety Patterns
proposedTopics.description: The defensive reflexes every contract needs: a pause switch for emergencies, reentrancy guards, and pull-over-push payments so one bad recipient can't wedge the whole system. These are the patterns that turn a discovered bug into a contained incident instead of a total loss.

proposedTopics.title: Signatures & Meta-Transactions
proposedTopics.description: Using off-chain signatures on-chain: ERC-2612 permit for gasless approvals, ERC-2771 meta-transactions for gasless UX, ERC-1271 so smart-contract wallets can 'sign', and the replay defenses (nonce, deadline, domain) that keep a signature from being reused. Builds on Phase 2's ECDSA/EIP-712 primitives.

proposedTopics.title: Distribution & Factory Patterns
proposedTopics.description: Getting tokens out and contracts deployed at scale: Merkle and signature airdrops that claim without storing every balance, multisig custody, and factory deployment via CREATE2 and EIP-1167 minimal-proxy clones. The common thread is doing per-user work cheaply and deterministically.

proposedTopics.title: DAOs & Governance
proposedTopics.description: On-chain governance: ERC-20Votes tokens with delegated, checkpointed voting power; the Governor framework's propose/vote/queue/execute lifecycle; and a Timelock that delays execution so users can exit before a malicious proposal lands.

proposedTopics.title: Pausable circuit breaker
proposedTopics.description: Pausable adds a boolean switch with whenNotPaused/whenPaused modifiers and _pause/_unpause, so a privileged account can freeze selected functions the moment a bug is spotted — a circuit breaker that buys time to respond. Add explicit access control to the internal pause functions, and think hard about which functions to gate: freezing deposits may contain damage, but freezing withdrawals can trap user funds.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Breaker.sol with a PAUSER_ROLE, whenNotPaused on deposit but an always-open emergencyWithdraw, plus test/phase04/Breaker.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a paused deposit reverts with EnforcedPause, unpause restores it, and users can still exit while paused. Threat: centralization — a pauser can freeze funds; and gating withdrawals can trap users, so keep an exit open.

requirements.purpose: Apply pause-state guards and explicit authorization to selected entry points

options.why: The current official API defines exactly what Pausable supplies and makes clear that callers must expose and authorize _pause and _unpause themselves.

proposedTopics.title: Reentrancy guard & checks-effects-interactions
proposedTopics.description: The primary defense against reentrancy is ordering — checks, then effects (update state), then interactions (external calls) — so a re-entrant call sees already-updated state. ReentrancyGuard's nonReentrant modifier adds one contract-wide guard around protected entry points; ReentrancyGuardTransient offers the same pattern on chains with EIP-1153 transient storage. Unguarded cross-function paths and read-only callbacks can still expose inconsistent state.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Bank.sol with a vulnerable withdraw and a fixed CEI+nonReentrant version, plus an Attacker.sol and test/phase04/Reentrancy.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the attacker drains the vulnerable contract and the reentrant call reverts (ReentrancyGuardReentrantCall) or nets zero against the fixed one. Threat: single-function, cross-function, and read-only reentrancy — CEI first, guard second. (cf. Ethernaut Reentrancy)

options.why: The language reference demonstrates the vulnerable ordering and the state-before-call repair exercised by the attack test.

proposedTopics.title: Pull-over-push payments
proposedTopics.description: Pushing funds — looping to send ETH to a list of recipients — fails when one recipient reverts (a contract with no receive, or a deliberate griefer), bricking the whole batch, and each external send is a reentrancy opening. Pull payments invert it: record what each account is owed in a mapping and let them withdraw individually, isolating failures and moving the external call to a single, guarded path. This is the standard fix for auction refunds and reward distribution.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Auction.sol where outbid refunds are credited to a pendingReturns mapping and withdrawn via a pull function, plus test/phase04/PullPayment.t.sol with a griefing bidder that reverts on receive. Done when: forge test proves the griefer cannot block other bidders, its failed withdrawal does not erase its credit, and another recipient can withdraw. Threat: push-payment DoS via a reverting recipient, and reentrancy on the send.

requirements.purpose: Replace recipient-driven push failure with isolated withdrawal credits

options.title: Solidity Common Patterns
options.scope: Section Withdrawal from Contracts
options.why: The official language guide contrasts a reverting push recipient with pending withdrawals and demonstrates clearing credit before transfer.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-2612 permit (gasless approvals)
proposedTopics.description: ERC-2612 adds permit(owner, spender, value, deadline, v, r, s) to an ERC-20, letting a user grant an allowance with an off-chain EIP-712 signature instead of a separate on-chain approve tx — so a dApp can approve-and-act in one transaction. Each owner has a monotonic nonce that the signature includes and permit increments, so a signature can't be replayed; the deadline bounds its validity. A permit can be submitted by anyone, so integrations should tolerate it being submitted before their bundled call when the intended allowance is already set. OZ's ERC20Permit implements it.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/PermitToken.sol extending OZ ERC20Permit, plus test/phase04/Permit.t.sol using vm.sign to build a valid permit. Done when: forge test proves a valid signature sets the allowance, replaying the same signature reverts (nonce consumed), and an expired deadline reverts. Threat: signature replay (guarded by nonce+deadline) and permit front-running — an integration that requires its permit call to succeed can be griefed after the same permit is submitted first.

requirements.purpose: Construct and test ERC-2612 permits with nonce, deadline, and domain checks

options.title: ERC-2612: Permit Extension for EIP-20 Signed Approvals

options.why: The final ERC defines the signed fields, nonce increment, deadline rule, approval effect, relayer option, front-running, censorship, and chain-split replay considerations.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-2771 meta-transactions
proposedTopics.description: ERC-2771 enables gasless UX: a user signs a request, a relayer pays gas and calls a trusted forwarder, and the target contract (using ERC2771Context) recovers the real user from the last 20 bytes the forwarder appends to calldata via _msgSender(). The security hinges entirely on trusting only a vetted forwarder — if an untrusted contract is trusted, it can append an arbitrary address and impersonate anyone. Use the Context accessors consistently in meta-transaction-aware logic.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Forwardable.sol using OZ ERC2771Context with an ERC2771Forwarder, plus test/phase04/MetaTx.t.sol relaying a signed request. Done when: forge test proves _msgSender() returns the signer (not the relayer) for a forwarded call and a direct call still reports the direct caller. Threat: trusting a malicious/unvetted forwarder → sender spoofing; and using msg.sender instead of _msgSender() breaks the abstraction.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-1271 contract signatures
proposedTopics.description: ecrecover only validates EOA signatures, so smart-contract wallets (Safe, ERC-4337 accounts) need a contract validation path. ERC-1271 defines isValidSignature(hash, signature) returning the magic value 0x1626ba7e when the contract considers the signature valid, letting the wallet implement its own scheme. OZ's SignatureChecker supports EOAs and contract signatures through one interface; unlike ECDSA signatures, a contract signature's validity can change over time.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/SmartWallet.sol with isValidSignature plus a consumer using OZ SignatureChecker, and test/phase04/Erc1271.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves SignatureChecker accepts a valid EOA signature and a valid contract (ERC-1271) signature, and rejects a bad one. Threat: an isValidSignature that doesn't bind the hash to a nonce/domain enables signature replay across contexts.

proposedTopics.title: Signature replay protection
proposedTopics.description: A bare signed message is a bearer token: without extra binding it can be replayed on the same contract, across chains, or across contracts. Consume a per-signer nonce for one-time use, add a deadline when authorization should expire, and use an EIP-712 domain containing chainId and verifyingContract to separate chains and verifiers. EIP-712 supplies domain separation but explicitly does not supply replay protection by itself.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/SignedActions.sol that executes an EIP-712-signed action guarded by a mapping nonce and a deadline, plus test/phase04/Replay.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a valid signed action executes once, a replay reverts (nonce spent), an expired deadline reverts, and a signature for another chainId reverts. Threat: same-contract / cross-chain / cross-contract replay — bind nonce + deadline + domain.

proposedTopics.title: Merkle-proof airdrops
proposedTopics.description: A Merkle airdrop commits to an eligibility list with one 32-byte root; each claim supplies a leaf and logarithmic-size proof, and the contract verifies it with MerkleProof.verify. This avoids preloading every allocation, though replay tracking still grows with successful claims. Encode the recipient and amount in the leaf and pay that recipient so a caller cannot redirect a claim; use an unambiguous leaf encoding (OpenZeppelin's StandardMerkleTree double-hashes leaves) so internal nodes cannot be reinterpreted as leaves.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/MerkleAirdrop.sol verifying claims against a root with a claimed mapping, plus test/phase04/MerkleAirdrop.t.sol building a tree and a proof. Done when: forge test proves a valid proof claims the exact amount once, a second claim reverts, and a forged/altered proof reverts. Threat: second-preimage leaf collision, double-claim, and claim front-running — hash leaves safely and bind the recipient.

requirements.purpose: Build compatible leaves and verify inclusion without ambiguous leaf preimages

proposedTopics.title: Signature-based airdrops
proposedTopics.description: An alternative to Merkle trees: an off-chain signer issues an EIP-712 authorization for a specific recipient, amount, nonce, and deadline, and the contract verifies it before paying out. It needs no on-chain root and lets eligibility be computed lazily, but centralizes issuance authority in the signer's key and needs explicit replay protection. SignatureChecker lets the authorized signer be either an EOA or a contract wallet.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/SigAirdrop.sol paying out on a valid signer EIP-712 signature guarded by a claimed nonce, plus test/phase04/SigAirdrop.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a valid signature from the authorized signer claims once, a replay reverts, and a signature from any other key reverts. Threat: signer-key compromise (mints unlimited claims), and signature replay without a per-claim nonce.

proposedTopics.title: Multisig wallets
proposedTopics.description: A multisig requires M-of-N owner approvals before a transaction executes: owners submit or sign, and execution proceeds once the threshold is met. A threshold above one removes any single owner key as sufficient authority; 1-of-N does not. Safe is a widely used implementation with modules and guards for extensibility. Enabled modules can bypass normal signature verification and execute arbitrary transactions, so module trust is part of the wallet's security boundary.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/MultiSig.sol with submit/confirm/execute over N owners and an M threshold, plus test/phase04/MultiSig.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a tx executes only after M confirmations, a non-owner cannot confirm, and a re-execution of an already-executed tx reverts. Threat: threshold misconfiguration (1-of-N) and owner-key compromise; and delegatecall modules can bypass the threshold if unvetted.

proposedTopics.title: CREATE2 deterministic deployment
proposedTopics.description: CREATE2 derives a contract's address from keccak256(0xff ‖ deployer ‖ salt ‖ keccak256(init_code))[12:], so the address depends on the deployer, salt, and init code rather than the deployer's nonce. This enables counterfactual addresses and the same address across chains only when those inputs match. EIP-6780 means SELFDESTRUCT normally no longer deletes existing code, so historical metamorphic redeployment assumptions no longer hold outside creation-and-destruction in one transaction.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Create2Factory.sol that deploys via create2 and a pure predictAddress helper, plus test/phase04/Create2.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves predictAddress equals the actual deployed address and redeploying with the same salt+init_code reverts (address taken). Threat: treating a counterfactual address as if code already exists or assuming cross-chain equality when the deployer or init code differs.

proposedTopics.title: Minimal-proxy clones (EIP-1167)
proposedTopics.description: ERC-1167 standardizes a 45-byte runtime proxy that delegates every call to a fixed implementation and bubbles return or revert data. OZ's Clones library deploys ordinary or deterministic clones and predicts deterministic addresses. Because construction initializes the implementation rather than each clone's storage, each clone needs its own initialization, ideally atomically in the factory.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/CloneFactory.sol using OZ Clones to spawn initialized instances of an implementation, plus test/phase04/Clones.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves each clone is independently initialized, shares the implementation's logic, and cloneDeterministic lands at the predicted address. Threat: an uninitialized clone (anyone can initialize it) — always initialize atomically in the factory.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-20Votes voting tokens
proposedTopics.description: ERC20Votes extends ERC-20 with delegation and checkpointed voting weight: getPastVotes(account, timepoint) reads an immutable past value so tokens transferred after a proposal snapshot cannot vote again from a new account. Tokens have no tracked voting power until delegated, including self-delegation. ERC-6372 clock() identifies the timepoint mode. Snapshotting prevents post-snapshot reuse, but it does not stop capital acquired or borrowed before the snapshot.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/GovToken.sol extending OZ ERC20Votes (+ERC20Permit), plus test/phase04/Votes.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves un-delegated tokens have 0 votes, delegating grants voting power, transfers move delegated power, and getPastVotes returns the immutable value at a past timepoint. Threat: double voting if governance reads current balances; economic takeover remains possible when voting power is acquired before the snapshot.

proposedTopics.title: Governor framework
proposedTopics.description: OZ Governor is a modular on-chain governance engine: propose() registers actions, voting starts after votingDelay, holders cast votes during votingPeriod using snapshot weight, and a successful proposal can be executed or queued first when a timelock module requires it. Modules supply vote counting, voting-power source, quorum, and execution policy. A proposalThreshold can limit who may propose.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/MyGovernor.sol composing GovernorVotes + GovernorCountingSimple + a quorum module over the GovToken, plus test/phase04/Governor.t.sol running a full propose→vote→execute. Done when: forge test proves a proposal below quorum fails, one above quorum with a For majority executes its action, and voting before delegation has no weight. Threat: governance takeover by voting power acquired before the snapshot; a timelock creates a reaction window but does not prevent capture.

proposedTopics.title: Timelock controller
proposedTopics.description: TimelockController enforces a minimum delay between scheduling and executing an operation, giving users a reaction window after governance decisions. PROPOSER_ROLE schedules, EXECUTOR_ROLE executes ready operations, and CANCELLER_ROLE cancels pending ones; granting EXECUTOR_ROLE to address(0) lets anyone execute a ready operation. In a Governor integration, governed assets and permissions belong to the timelock because it performs the eventual calls.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Timelock.sol wiring OZ TimelockController as the executor for MyGovernor, plus test/phase04/Timelock.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a scheduled operation reverts if executed before minDelay, succeeds after warping past it, and only the CANCELLER can cancel a pending op. Threat: a zero minDelay or mis-set PROPOSER/EXECUTOR roles removes the exit window entirely.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Pausable give you, and which functions should you be careful NOT to gate?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pause state, whenNotPaused/whenPaused modifiers, and internal _pause/_unpause functions that you authorize and apply to selected entry points. Pitfall: Pausable does not pause functions automatically, and gating withdrawals/exits can trap user funds — pause deposits and risky actions but leave an emergency exit open.

proposedPrompts.promptText: State the checks-effects-interactions order and why nonReentrant alone isn't enough.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Checks (validate) → Effects (update state) → Interactions (external calls), so a re-entrant call sees finalized state. OZ nonReentrant uses one contract-wide guard, so reentry into any protected entry point fails; it cannot protect an unguarded sibling or prevent another protocol from reading transiently inconsistent state during a callback. Pitfall: apply CEI first and guard every exposed mutation that shares the invariant.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Rewrite a vulnerable withdraw to be reentrancy-safe with CEI.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 amt = balance[msg.sender]; balance[msg.sender] = 0; (bool ok,) = msg.sender.call{value: amt}(""); require(ok); — zero the balance (effect) BEFORE the external call (interaction), so a re-entrant withdraw sees 0.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve the Ethernaut Reentrancy level: drain a contract whose withdraw sends before it debits.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Deposit a small amount, then in your attacker's receive/fallback call withdraw again while your recorded balance is still non-zero; the contract sends ETH before zeroing your balance, so each re-entry pays you again until it's empty. Fix is CEI + nonReentrant.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is looping to push payments dangerous, and what does the pull pattern change?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: One recipient that reverts (no receive, or a griefer) makes the whole loop revert, and each send is a reentrancy opening — a push refund can DoS everyone. Pull payments credit a mapping and let each account withdraw itself, isolating failures and reducing external calls to one guarded path. Pitfall: still apply CEI on the withdraw.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does permit avoid a separate approve tx, and what stops the signature being replayed?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The owner signs an EIP-712 permit(owner,spender,value,deadline) off-chain; anyone submits it and the token sets the allowance, so approve+action fit in one tx. A per-owner nonce (included and incremented) blocks replay and the deadline bounds validity. Pitfall: anyone can submit the permit first, so an integration should tolerate its permit call failing when the intended allowance is already set.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In an ERC-2771 contract, why read _msgSender() instead of msg.sender, and where is the trust?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: For a forwarded call msg.sender is the relayer/forwarder; the real user is appended to the last 20 bytes of calldata and recovered by _msgSender(). Trust rests entirely on only whitelisting a vetted forwarder. Pitfall: trusting an untrusted contract lets it append any address and impersonate anyone, and mixing raw msg.sender into logic breaks the abstraction.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does ERC-1271 exist, and how should a verifier support both EOAs and contract wallets?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: ecrecover only validates EOA ECDSA sigs, so smart-contract wallets expose isValidSignature(hash,sig) returning the magic value 0x1626ba7e when they accept a signature. Use OZ SignatureChecker, which uses ECDSA for an EOA signer and ERC-1271 when the signer has code. Pitfall: an isValidSignature that doesn't bind hash to a nonce/domain lets a signature be replayed.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Name the three ways a signed message can be replayed and the defense for each.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Same-contract replay → a per-signer nonce the contract consumes; cross-chain replay → chainId in the EIP-712 domain separator; cross-contract replay → verifyingContract in the domain separator (plus a deadline to bound the window). Pitfall: omitting any one — especially the nonce — turns a signature into a reusable bearer token.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a Merkle airdrop scale, and what two disciplines keep it safe?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Store one root instead of preloading every allocation; each claim submits a recipient-and-amount leaf plus a logarithmic proof and records replay state only when claimed. Use an unambiguous leaf encoding (StandardMerkleTree double-hashes) so an internal node cannot masquerade as a leaf, and pay the recipient encoded in the leaf so a caller cannot redirect funds. Pitfall: forgetting replay tracking allows double claims.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the core of an OZ MerkleProof airdrop claim check.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 leaf = keccak256(bytes.concat(keccak256(abi.encode(msg.sender, amount)))); require(!claimed[msg.sender]); require(MerkleProof.verify(proof, root, leaf)); claimed[msg.sender] = true; — double-hashed leaf, claimed flag set before transfer.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a signature airdrop differ from a Merkle airdrop, and what's its main risk?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Instead of an on-chain root + proof, an off-chain signer issues an EIP-712 signature authorizing (address, amount); the contract verifies it and pays out — no root needed, eligibility computed lazily. Risk: it centralizes trust in the signer's key (a leak mints unlimited claims). Pitfall: needs a per-claim nonce + deadline or the signature is replayable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What security property does an M-of-N multisig provide, and what are its dangerous settings?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It requires M of N owner approvals to execute; when M > 1, no single owner key is sufficient. Pitfall: 1-of-N keeps a single-key failure mode, owner and threshold changes are security-critical, and an enabled Safe module can execute arbitrary transactions without the normal signature check. Guards inspect transactions but are not the same authority path as modules.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Give the CREATE2 address formula and one thing it enables that CREATE does not.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: address = keccak256(0xff ‖ deployer ‖ salt ‖ keccak256(init_code))[12:]. Independent of the deployer's nonce, so you can compute the address before deployment; matching deployer, salt, and init code can produce the same address across chains. Pitfall: a precomputed address may have no code yet, and EIP-6780 ended general CREATE2 redeployment after later SELFDESTRUCT.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is an EIP-1167 clone, and why must you initialize it after deploying?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A ~45-byte proxy that delegatecalls a hard-coded implementation, so deploying the Nth identical instance is cheap (OZ Clones.clone / cloneDeterministic). Because it's a proxy, the implementation's constructor never runs against the clone's storage — you must call an initializer after cloning. Pitfall: leaving a clone uninitialized lets anyone initialize (and hijack) it, so initialize atomically in the factory.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why doesn't holding ERC20Votes tokens give you voting power, and how does it resist flash-loan voting?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Voting power is tracked by delegation, so you must delegate to yourself or another account before tokens count. getPastVotes fixes weight at the proposal snapshot, preventing later transfers from reusing the same tokens; power acquired after the snapshot cannot affect that vote. Pitfall: snapshotting does not stop power acquired or borrowed before the snapshot, and current balance is not a safe vote source.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Walk the OZ Governor proposal lifecycle and name what weights the votes.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: propose() → votingDelay → holders cast For/Against/Abstain over votingPeriod, weighted by getPastVotes at the snapshot → if quorum + majority, execute the encoded calls, queueing first when a timelock module is configured. proposalThreshold gates who can propose. Pitfall: tokens must be delegated before the snapshot block/timestamp to count.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does a governance Timelock protect against, and who holds the protocol in a Governor+Timelock setup?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It enforces minDelay between scheduling and execution, creating a reaction window. In a Governor integration the Timelock owns governed assets and permissions because it executes the proposal calls; the Governor is normally a proposer. PROPOSER, EXECUTOR, and CANCELLER roles separate duties, and granting EXECUTOR_ROLE to address(0) permits anyone to execute ready operations. Pitfall: zero delay or unsafe role grants remove the intended control.
